claim: The human genome encodes >500 kinases.
source: the human genome encodes >500 kinases (Manning et al., 2002b)
evidence: Supported by citation to Manning et al., 2002b

claim: Over 100,000 phosphorylation sites have been identified.
source: over 100,000 phosphorylation sites have been identified (Hornbeck et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hornbeck et al., 2012

claim: The number and diversity of kinases expanded with increasing numbers of cell types during the evolution of metazoa.
source: The number and diversity of kinases expanded with increasing numbers of cell types during the evolution of metazoa (Manning et al., 2002a)
evidence: Supported by citation to Manning et al., 2002a

claim: The addition of new kinase families with new specificities presumably increases the information processing capacity of the cell.
source: The addition of new kinase families with new specificities presumably increases the information processing capacity of the cell, thus enabling the emergence of more complex biological processes (Beltrao et al., 2009; Lim and Pawson, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Beltrao et al., 2009 and Lim and Pawson, 2010, and involves speculative reasoning about the functional consequences

claim: Phosphorylation reactions act on time scales of minutes.
source: phosphorylation reactions act on time scales of minutes (Olsen et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Olsen et al., 2006

claim: Within substrates, the gain or loss of kinase interaction motifs and phosphorylation sites have occurred relatively rapidly (changes occur within a few millions of years of divergence).
source: Within substrates, the gain or loss of kinase interaction motifs and phosphorylation sites have occurred relatively rapidly (changes occur within a few millions of years of divergence, Holt et al., 2009; Beltrao et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to Holt et al., 2009 and Beltrao et al., 2009

claim: Kinases act as hubs of phosphoregulatory networks and can coordinate the activities of hundreds or even thousands of substrates.
source: Kinases act as hubs of phosphoregulatory networks and can coordinate the activities of hundreds or even thousands of substrates (Manning et al., 2002a; Matsuoka et al., 2007; Holt et al., 2009; Hornbeck et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Manning et al., 2002a; Matsuoka et al., 2007; Holt et al., 2009; Hornbeck et al., 2012

claim: S. cerevisiae Ime2 and mouse ICK differ in their +1 specificities.
source: previous work has shown that S. cerevisiae Ime2 and mouse ICK differ in their +1 specificities (Fu et al., 2006; Holt et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to Fu et al., 2006 and Holt et al., 2007

claim: All kinases in the IME2/RCK/LF4 superfamily share a strong preference for arginine at the −3 position and proline at the −2 position.
source: As previously reported for S. cerevisiae Ime2 and mouse ICK, PSPL analysis revealed that all kinases assayed share a strong preference for arginine at the −3 position and proline at the −2 position (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from PSPL analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2

claim: The preferred residue at the +1 position varied between arginine (+1R) for the S. cerevisiae, Candida glabrata, and Yarrowia lipolytica Ime2 homologs and proline (+1P) for the three mammalian RCK kinases.
source: Specifically, the preferred residue at the +1 position varied between arginine (+1R) for the S. cerevisiae, Candida glabrata, and Yarrowia lipolytica Ime2 homologs and proline (+1P) for the three mammalian RCK kinases
evidence: Supported by experimental data from PSPL analysis

claim: Neurospora crassa Ime2 and Naegleria gruberi LF4 phosphorylated peptides with +1R and +1P relatively equally.
source: Neurospora crassa Ime2 and Naegleria gruberi LF4 phosphorylated peptides with +1R and +1P relatively equally (Figure 1C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: S. cerevisiae Ime2 phosphorylated the +1R peptide with 65-fold greater efficiency (kcat/KM) than the corresponding +1P peptide.
source: S. cerevisiae Ime2 phosphorylated the +1R peptide with 65-fold greater efficiency (kcat/KM) than the corresponding +1P peptide
evidence: Supported by experimental kinetic data shown in Figure 1B and Table 1

claim: N. gruberi homolog LF4 phosphorylated the +1R and +1P peptides with similar kinetics.
source: the N. gruberi homolog LF4 phosphorylated the +1R and +1P peptides with similar kinetics
evidence: Supported by experimental kinetic data shown in Table 1

claim: Mouse MOK showed a twofold preference for the +1P peptide.
source: mouse MOK showed a twofold preference for the +1P peptide (Table 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental kinetic data shown in Table 1

claim: AncCMGI had a well-defined primary specificity, with a strong preference for arginine at the −3 position and proline at the −2 position.
source: However, we observed that AncCMGI had a well-defined primary specificity, with a strong preference for arginine at the −3 position and proline at the −2 position (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by experimental PSPL data shown in Figure 2B

claim: AncCMGI displayed a 5.6-fold preference for proline at the +1 position.
source: AncCMGI could phosphorylate peptides having either a proline or an arginine residue at the +1 position, though it displayed a 5.6-fold preference for proline (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: AncCMGI does not require cyclin for activity.
source: Furthermore, AncCMGI does not appear to require cyclin for activity (as with CDKs): we observed no significant co-purifying proteins, and E. coli does not encode any cyclin orthologs (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and inference from E. coli lacking cyclin orthologs

claim: AncCMGI contains a MAPK-like TXY motif in the activation loop.
source: In addition, AncCMGI contains a MAPK-like TXY motif in the activation loop
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis of the reconstructed ancestor

claim: AncCMGI is likely activated through autophosphorylation, similar to extant mammalian DYRK and GSK family kinases.
source: Because E. coli lack endogenous kinases capable of phosphorylating this TXY motif, AncCMGI is likely activated through autophosphorylation, similar to extant mammalian DYRK and GSK family kinases (Cole et al., 2004; Lochhead et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by inference from E. coli lacking appropriate kinases and citation to Cole et al., 2004 and Lochhead et al., 2005

claim: AncCMGI appears to have preferred +1P substrates.
source: As described above, AncCMGI appears to have preferred +1P substrates
evidence: Supported by experimental data from peptide assays shown in Figure 3B,C

claim: On the phylogenetic branch leading to the common ancestor of the IME2/RCK/LF4 group (i.e., AncNgru), the +1 specificity relaxed to equally accommodate both +1R and +1P (+1PR).
source: On the phylogenetic branch leading to the common ancestor of the IME2/RCK/LF4 group (i.e., AncNgru), the +1 specificity relaxed to equally accommodate both +1R and +1P (+1PR)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from peptide assays shown in Figure 3B,C

claim: The specificity reverted to the ancestral +1P-preferring state along the branch leading to the mammalian RCK kinases (ICK and MAK).
source: Namely, the specificity reverted to the ancestral +1P-preferring state along the branch leading to the mammalian RCK kinases (ICK and MAK)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from peptide assays shown in Figure 3

claim: The specificity shifted to +1R in the fungal lineage leading to the ancestor of the IME2 kinases (i.e., AncIME2).
source: In contrast, the specificity shifted to +1R in the fungal lineage leading to the ancestor of the IME2 kinases (i.e., AncIME2)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from peptide assays shown in Figure 3

claim: AncIME2 had a moderate preference for +1R.
source: AncIME2 had a moderate preference for +1R
evidence: Supported by experimental data from peptide assays shown in Figure 3

claim: The nature of the phosphoacceptor affects +1 specificity: serine causes a shift towards +1R preference, while threonine causes a shift towards +1P preference.
source: From these experiments, we found that, indeed, the phosphoacceptor affects +1 specificity: serine causes a shift towards +1R preference, while threonine causes a shift towards +1P preference (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: This dependence of +1 specificity on the phosphoacceptor is present in AncCMGI and is maintained in all ancestors and extant members of the IME2/RCK/LF4 family.
source: This dependence of +1 specificity on the phosphoacceptor is present in AncCMGI and is maintained in all ancestors and extant members of the IME2/RCK/LF4 family (Figures 3B and 4C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B, 4C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: The amino acid immediately C-terminal to the conserved DFG motif contributes to preference for serine vs threonine at the phosphoacceptor.
source: Previous work revealed that the amino acid immediately C-terminal to the conserved DFG motif contributes to preference for serine vs threonine at the phosphoacceptor (Chen et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2014

claim: The DFGx residue was a leucine in AncCMGI and then mutated to serine multiple times in the CMGC family.
source: Our ancestral reconstructions indicate that the DFGx residue was a leucine in AncCMGI and then mutated to serine multiple times in the CMGC family (Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by ancestral reconstruction data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The presence of leucine vs serine at DFGx in present-day kinases correlates with specificity for +1P vs +1R.
source: Further, the presence of leucine vs serine at DFGx in present-day kinases correlates with specificity for +1P vs +1R
evidence: Supported by comparison of sequence and specificity data across kinases

claim: A single mutation at DFGx (L146S) made ICK approximately threefold more proline specific.
source: This single mutation at DFGx made ICK approximately threefold more proline specific, such that its specificity resembled that of MOK (Figure 4C)
evidence: Supported by experimental mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Mutating the DFGx residue in MOK (S148L) had the reverse effect of converting MOK from +1P preference to a non-selective kinase (+1PR).
source: Conversely, mutating the DFGx residue in the opposite direction in MOK (S148L) had the reverse effect of converting MOK from +1P preference to a non-selective kinase (+1PR)
evidence: Supported by experimental mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4C

claim: In all cases, mutation from leucine to serine at DFGx shifted kinase function towards +1P specificity, while mutation from serine to leucine at DFGx shifted the kinases towards +1R specificity.
source: In all cases, we observed that mutation from leucine to serine at DFGx shifted kinase function towards +1P specificity, while mutation from serine to leucine at DFGx shifted the kinases towards +1R specificity (Figure 4C)
evidence: Supported by experimental mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Ime2 is expressed exclusively during meiosis in S. cerevisiae.
source: In S. cerevisiae, Ime2 is expressed exclusively during meiosis
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about Ime2 expression

claim: Ime2 is required for all stages of meiosis, including meiotic initiation, S-phase, the meiotic divisions, and gametogenesis.
source: Ime2 is expressed exclusively during meiosis and is required for all stages of this process, including meiotic initiation, S-phase, the meiotic divisions, and gametogenesis (Yoshida et al., 1990; Dirick et al., 1998; Benjamin, 2003; Holt et al., 2007; McDonald et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to Yoshida et al., 1990; Dirick et al., 1998; Benjamin, 2003; Holt et al., 2007; McDonald et al., 2009

claim: A kinase-dead version of Ime2 (ime2-K97R) failed to support meiosis.
source: As reported previously (Benjamin, 2003), a kinase-dead version of Ime2 (ime2-K97R) failed to support meiosis (not shown)
evidence: Supported by citation to Benjamin, 2003 and experimental observation

claim: Cells with both copies of IME2 replaced with a DFGx mutant (ime2-L231S) completed meiosis, but with a reduction of sporulation efficiency.
source: However, cells with both copies of IME2 replaced with a DFGx mutant (ime2-L231S) completed meiosis, but with a reduction of sporulation efficiency thus indicating that the ime2-DFGx allele has significant activity in vivo (Figure 5A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The homozygous ime2-DFGx cells that did correctly form tetrads had reduced spore viability.
source: The homozygous ime2-DFGx cells that did correctly form tetrads had reduced spore viability (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Homozygous ime2-DFGx cells initiated S-phase and the meiotic divisions with a 2–3 hr delay.
source: initiated S-phase (Figure 5C) and the meiotic divisions (Figure 5D) with a 2–3 hr delay
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and 5D

claim: IME2/ime2-DFGx heterozygous strains had no noticeable defects in meiosis or sporulation.
source: IME2/ime2-DFGx strains had no noticeable defects in meiosis or sporulation. DNA replication and divisions occurred on schedule, spore formation was normal, and spore viability was high (Figure 5)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: The defects seen in the homozygous DFGx mutant strains are most likely due to weakening of network connections, rather than the creation of new deleterious phosphorylation sites.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the defects seen in the homozygous DFGx mutant strains are most likely due to weakening of network connections, rather than the creation of new deleterious phosphorylation sites
evidence: Inferred from the observation that heterozygous strains show no defects

claim: The meiotic phosphoregulatory network can tolerate divergence of specificity in a second copy of the IME2 gene.
source: This experiment is analogous to gene duplication followed by paralog divergence in evolution and indicates that the meiotic phosphoregulatory network can tolerate divergence of specificity in a second copy of the IME2 gene
evidence: Inferred from the heterozygous experiment results

claim: The ancestor of all CMGC kinases had slight specificity for proline at its +1 site (+1P).
source: The ancestor of all CMGC kinases had slight specificity for proline at its +1 site (+1P)
evidence: Supported by experimental characterization of resurrected AncCMGI

claim: The evolutionary trajectory from +1P to +1R passed through a historic ancestor with hybrid +1PR specificity.
source: Taken together with the measured specificities of reconstructed CMGC kinases, these results suggest that the evolutionary trajectory from +1P to +1R passed through a historic ancestor with hybrid +1PR specificity
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data on ancestral kinases and mutants

claim: AncCMGI does not require a cyclin or any C-terminal extension for its activation.
source: In fact, we observed that AncCMGI, the maximum likelihood common ancestor of CDK, CDKL, MAPK, GSK, and IME2/RCK/LF4, has essentially the same specificity as the mouse MOK kinase and does not require a cyclin or any C-terminal extension for its activation
evidence: Supported by experimental characterization of AncCMGI

claim: Cyclin dependence is a derived characteristic.
source: Our phylogenetic reconstructions indicate, therefore, that cyclin dependence is a derived characteristic
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AncCMGI does not require cyclin

claim: Selectivity for proline at the +1 position is a unique characteristic of the CMGC group.
source: Selectivity for proline at the +1 position is a unique characteristic of the CMGC group, as kinases from other groups appear to strongly disfavor proline (Zhu et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2005

claim: This proline selectivity has been attributed to an arginine residue found at the C-terminus of the activation loop (at the xAPE position) that is unique to the CMCG group.
source: This proline selectivity has been attributed to an arginine residue found at the C-terminus of the activation loop (at the xAPE position) that is unique to the CMCG group
evidence: Based on established structural knowledge about CMGC kinases

claim: The DFGx residue is one determinant of +1 specificity.
source: We have identified the DFGx residue as one such determinant
evidence: Supported by experimental mutagenesis data

claim: Kinases display little inter-positional dependence in their primary peptide specificity.
source: Computational analyses have suggested that kinases display little inter-positional dependence in their primary peptide specificity and that each substrate peptide amino acid interacts with the kinase active site more or less independently (Joughin et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Joughin et al., 2012

claim: The observation that +1 specificity is dependent on the identity of the phosphoacceptor represents an exception to the model that kinases display little inter-positional dependence.
source: Our observation that +1 specificity is dependent on the identity of the phosphoacceptor represents an exception to this model
evidence: Inferred from the experimental observation of inter-positional dependence

claim: This inter-positional dependence is ancestral and has been maintained in the entire IME2/RCK/LF4 family of kinases.
source: This inter-positional dependence is ancestral and has been maintained in the entire IME2/RCK/LF4 family of kinases
evidence: Supported by experimental data across ancestral and extant kinases

claim: The common role for the DFGx residue in influencing specificity for both the +1 and phosphoacceptor residues provides a structural basis for inter-dependence between the two positions.
source: The common role for the DFGx residue in influencing specificity for both the +1 and phosphoacceptor residues provides a structural basis for inter-dependence between the two positions
evidence: Inferred from experimental mutagenesis data and structural considerations

claim: CMGC kinases seem to be relatively tolerant to modulation of +1 specificity by mutation of the DFGx residue.
source: CMGC kinases seem to be relatively tolerant to modulation of +1 specificity by mutation of the DFGx residue: this mutation did not lead to a significant loss of activity in any of the six kinases we tested
evidence: Supported by experimental mutagenesis data across multiple kinases

claim: This is an unusual case where a single amino acid mutation can drive divergence of specificity without the need for additional stabilizing mutations.
source: This is an unusual case where a single amino acid mutation can drive divergence of specificity without the need for additional stabilizing mutations
evidence: Inferred from the observation that DFGx mutations shift specificity without loss of activity

claim: Following AncCMGI, a gene duplication occurred, and the specificities of the two descendant paralogs almost completely diverged.
source: Following AncCMGI, a gene duplication occurred, and the specificities of the two descendant paralogs almost completely diverged
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic analysis and specificity data

claim: Cdk1 recognizes a [S/T*]-P-x-[K/R] motif.
source: Cdk1 recognizes a [S/T*]-P-x-[K/R] motif
evidence: Based on established knowledge about Cdk1 specificity

claim: Ime2 recognizes R-P-x-[S/T*]-R motif.
source: while its paralog Ime2 recognizes R-P-x-[S/T*]-R (Figure 2A; Holt et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Holt et al., 2007 and Figure 2A

claim: Expansion of Ime2 specificity is not highly toxic to cells as long as a wild-type copy of IME2 is present.
source: However, our initial genetic analysis of the DFGx mutant suggests that expansion of Ime2 specificity is not highly toxic to cells. As long as a wild-type copy of IME2 is present, the second copy can expand its activity without any noticeable reduction of meiotic efficiency
evidence: Supported by experimental data from heterozygous strains

claim: The DFGx specificity mutation is observed in multiple cancer kinases including Aurora A, PKCgamma, Haspin, DDR1, ITK, TRKA, IRAK3 and BRAF.
source: During the process of submission the authors have learned that the DFGx specificity mutation described in this study is also observed in multiple cancer kinases including Aurora A, PKCgamma, Haspin, DDR1, ITK, TRKA, IRAK3 and BRAF (Creixell et al. unpublished)
evidence: Supported by citation to unpublished work by Creixell et al.

claim: Amino acid changes that occur during evolution are resampled in cancer.
source: suggesting that amino acid changes that occur during evolution are resampled in cancer
evidence: Speculative inference from the observation of DFGx mutations in cancer kinases
